newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hong Kong activists leave Japan seas after protest.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong activists leave Japan seas after protest.

text.p: Three Hong Kong and Taiwanese activists on Monday made dramatic leaps from their boats onto Japanese coastguard vessels in a high seas standoff over ownership of disputed islands.

A Japanese spokesman said after hours of playing cat-and-mouse, which resulted in several minor collisions, a flotilla of about 20 Hong Kong and Taiwanese boats abandoned their efforts to break through a coastguard cordon of 60 vessels, some armed, and land on the islands in the East China Sea.

The dispute is over islands called the Senkakus in Japanese that Taiwan and China claim as the Diaoyus. The islands lie about 200 km (125 miles) north-east of Taiwan and south-west of Japan's southern island chain of Okinawa.
Two Hong Kong activists who leapt from the flotilla flagship called "Protect-the-Diaoyus" onto a coastguard ship were handed over to a Taiwanese media vessel, a Japanese official said.
A third protester who jumped from a Taiwanese boat onto another coastguard ship was returned to the flotilla earlier, the official said.
None of the three was arrested, despite Japan's warning it would seize boats and deal strictly with activists who violated Japan's maritime borders and immigration laws.

The Hong Kong-Taiwan flotilla was protesting near the uninhabited islands when they were blocked by the Japanese coastguard fleet. The spokesman said some of the vessels bumped each other but were not seriously damaged.
He said some protest ships entered the 12-nautical mile territorial waters claimed by Japan but none was seized, as top Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama had warned.

"The Japanese government will take appropriate measures to block (the activists) from landing on the islands," Kajiyama told a news conference earlier. Asked if the measures could include seizing the ships, Kajiyama replied: "Yes, that's right."
"As we have repeatedly said, the islands are Japan's territory and they are effectively controlled by Japan," Kajiyama said.
"Therefore, landing on the islands would constitute a violation of Japan's law."
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters: "We must not let them into our territorial waters."

The dispute over sovereignty has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese rightist group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands in July 1996.
A Hong Kong activist drowned in September when he jumped from a protest boat into rough seas during an abortive voyage to the islands.

In a move that fuelled the dispute, four Japanese, including a legislator, planted a Japanese flag on one of the islands earlier this month and spent two hours surveying and holding a memorial ceremony.
Japan took over the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. China and Taiwan say they should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
